transcript:
Meeting header: HeliosRetail POC weekly sync - Cost/unit economics and tuning. Recorded 2026-09-29 16:00 PDT. Duration approx 38m. Redwood: Jordan Kim (AE), Priya Singh (SE). HeliosRetail: Maya Ortiz (CTO), Liam Nguyen (ML Eng), Ravi Patel (Infra), Sofia Chen (Product).

Summary: Quick review of pilot numbers (tokens/sec/$), caching impact, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run cache warmup for Top-50 queries, tighten batching windows for low-latency routes, and share a tokens-per-dollar workbook. Discussed potential dedicated slots vs hosted bursts for peak traffic. next steps and owners at end.

Topics: cost per 1k tokens, tokens/sec per dollar, p95 latency vs batching window, KV/prefix cache effectiveness, quantization tradeoffs, SOC2/data residency question.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Jordan from Redwood, Priya here as our SE. Maya?
[00:10] Maya: Hi Jordan, hi Priya. Maya here. Liam on as well.
[00:15] Liam: Yup hey, Liam. Sorry running a little late to the last bit.
[00:20] Jordan: No worries. Agenda — pick up where we left: look at the last 48h of pilot metrics, talk caching numbers and batching knobs, decide next steps.
[00:31] Priya: I'll share my screen — pulling the tokens-per-dollar dashboard and the KV cache hit-rate for the Top-100 routes. Note: a couple of labels may be off in the export, I think it says "Redwood Inferance" in one chart, ignore that.
[01:05] Maya: ha, that's fine.
[01:12] Priya: Alright, metrics first: overall tokens/sec per dollar for the baseline model (redwood-3-small-quant) was ~1,250 tokens/$ on average across the window, but with large spread. With prefix caching enabled for the Top-20 queries hit-rate moved to 34% and tokens/$ improved to ~1,640 tokens/$. So roughly a 30% lift from caching alone.
[01:50] Ravi: Where are you measuring that — p50 or p95?
[01:54] Priya: Good call. That's an average (mean) tokens per dollar across all requests. For p95 latency at the same config we saw 220ms without batching, 320ms with a 50ms batching hold (higher throughput but added tail).
[02:20] Liam: So with batching the tokens/$ goes up but latency p95 worsens, right?
[02:26] Priya: Exactly. Example: turning batching window to 25ms gave tokens/$ ~1,420 and p95 ~260ms. At 0ms (no explicit batching) tokens/$ ~1,250 and p95 ~210ms. It's the classic throughput vs latency tradeoff.
[02:45] Jordan: Can you remind folks what the cost baseline is? I sent the raw numbers in the sheet but quick reminder — GPU-backed serving cost here is modeled as effective $/sec based on instance amortization and token time.
[02:58] Priya: Yes, baseline used our shared-hosted compute estimate with mixed quantization. If you want dedicated slots, that changes the fixed cost and improves tokens/$ for sustained high QPS.
[03:15] Maya: We're mostly worried about interactive flows — we need p95 < 250ms for checkout suggestions. So latency is critical on key routes. But for downstream batch scoring, cost matters more.
[03:30] Sofia: Right — product priority is 70% interactive, 30% async scoring. So we need to tune per-route.
[03:40] Priya: Good segmentation. We recommend split routing — low-latency route with minimal batching and dedicated capacity during peaks, and a cost-optimized route with aggressive batching and cache-first for non-critical queries.
[03:58] Ravi: On the KV cache: is the warmup effect mostly prefix reuse or full KV reuse? We saw week-over-week hit-rate improve.
[04:06] Priya: It's a mix. For HeliosRetail the top 50 queries are repeated language patterns — prefix KV caching yields biggest wins. Full KV cache (longer-lived session cache) helps for chatty sessions but has more memory cost. The warmup test we propose is 6 hours of synthetic replay to prepopulate the KV store for top patterns.
[04:35] Liam: If we prewarm, what's the expected latency delta for a cached hit?
[04:39] Priya: Cached token generation path reduces compute ~18-25% for those tokens because KV lookups avoid recompute; user-observed latency for the cached prefix tokens drops by ~30ms on average — varies by model and quantization.
[04:55] Maya: That sounds promising. Any downsides? Memory, eviction policies?
[05:00] Priya: Memory and cold-start complexity. Also cache consistency if model version changes; we recommend versioned caches and a migration window.
[05:12] Jordan: Let's talk quantization next — we ran 4-bit vs 8-bit earlier this morning?
[05:18] Priya: Yes. 4-bit quant gives ~20% faster token throughput in our bench but quality regressions on some prompt families (short-form instruction prompts). 8-bit qram is a safer compromise — we saw ~10% throughput gain with negligible quality delta. For HeliosRetail I'd suggest 8-bit on interactive route, and 4-bit for async scoring if you can tolerate slight drop.
[05:46] Liam: Can we do hybrid per-route quantization? i.e., interactive model = 8-bit, batch model = 4-bit?
[05:51] Priya: Absolutely. That's standard. Redwood routing can map routes to model variants.
[05:57] Jordan: Also worth calling out that with dedicated capacity, the unit economics improve because fixed costs amortize, so 4-bit becomes more attractive on sustained load.
[06:10] Maya: Do you have a simple break-even calc?
[06:13] Jordan: We'll put that into the tokens-per-dollar sheet. Quick back-of-envelope: if more than ~7k sustained qps for a route, dedicated and 4-bit usually wins. We'll share the precise break-even in the workbook.
[06:28] Sofia: How did the real traffic compare to our sample? We changed the sample set last week — any drift?
[06:33] Priya: Real traffic skewed heavier on the recommendations route; our sample underweighted long sessions. Liam, the distribution you send this week will help.
[06:40] Liam: Will do — I'll add session length histograms.
[06:44] [07:00] Jordan: Ok let's walk through the last 48h anomalies — there was a spike in cost on Tuesday night.
[07:06] Priya: Right — we saw a burst of long-form scoring tasks hitting the hosted route which caused short-lived autoscaling to spin more GPUs. The sheet flags CPU-bound preprocessing as the root cause — preprocessing is upstream and not Redwood, but it increased average token length per request and thus cost.
[07:28] Ravi: We're moving that preprocessing into a lambda that pre-trims tokens — should reduce the payload length.
[07:35] Priya: Good. That would lower tokens generated per request and help tokens/$ directly.
[07:40] Maya: On routing — do you support dynamic routing policies by time-of-day or traffic percent?
[07:45] Jordan: Yes, you can set routing policy rules. Example: route 95% of non-critical scoring to cost-optimized pool during midnight hours.
[07:55] Priya: We also have fallback rules — if dedicated pool is saturated we can route to hosted variant with slightly higher cost but maintained availability.
[08:04] Liam: Any implications for stateful chat sessions when failover happens?
[08:08] Priya: For stateful sessions we keep session metadata in a secure store; however KV caches won't transfer seamlessly. We'll add a note: session affinity preferred for chatty flows.
[08:20] [09:00] Sofia: On the security/compliance front, our InfoSec wants to see audit logs and KMS integration.
[09:06] Jordan: We provided the SOC2 artifact link in the doc earlier — it's the same set plus per-route audit logs. For KMS, Redwood supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). We'll email the checklist.
[09:20] Maya: Great. Also, data residency: can we pin a region?
[09:24] Priya: Yes, you can pin to the us-west-2 region or request on-prem if needed. For HeliosRetail US-west region is supported.
[09:33] [10:00] Priya: Quick demo of the tokens workbook: showing per-model row, tokens generated, compute seconds, effective $/token, tokens per dollar, and p95 latency.
[10:12] Jordan: Note that the workbook includes two columns: cached-adjusted tokens/$ (accounts for cache hit savings) and naive tokens/$. Use the cached-adjusted for route-level decisions.
[10:22] Liam: How do you compute cache-adjusted?
[10:24] Priya: We multiply the cache hit-rate by the per-token compute saved and subtract from total compute. Example: 34% hit-rate * 0.22 token compute savings etc. The sheet has the exact formula in the notes tab.
[10:36] Sofia: Can you link the spreadsheet?
[10:38] Jordan: I'll drop the link in the follow-up and in the shared notes — looks like I already uploaded a v2 in the drive link: https://redwood.example.com/drive/helios-tokens-v2 (internal link).
[10:52] [12:00] Maya: Priya, can you run a quick runbook item: what to change in config to hit <250ms p95 on interactive route?
[12:07] Priya: Sure — short answer: reduce batching window to 10-15ms for that route, use 8-bit quantization, ensure prewarm KV cache for top prefixes, and pin to dedicated slots during peak. I'll write a config snippet and post it.
[12:26] Jordan: We'll also recommend a canary: run the new config for 2 hours during a traffic window and monitor p95 and tokens/$.
[12:36] Liam: For canary, can we limit to 5% of traffic?
[12:39] Priya: Yes — canary supports percentage-based splits.
[12:43] [14:00] Maya: On cost — what's the expected improvement if we increase cache hit-rate from 34% to 55%?
[14:07] Priya: Ballpark: tokens/$ could improve another ~22-25% depending on which tokens are cached. If those cached tokens are the heavy-left part of sessions, the effect is higher. We should model by route.
[14:25] Jordan: We'll add a scenario tab in the sheet modeling 40/55/70% hit-rate.
[14:30] Ravi: Is it straightforward to increase hit-rate? That usually means standardizing prompts more or moving normalization upstream.
[14:36] Liam: We'll work on prompt normalization. Also need to see if personalization variables can be separated so prefix reuse increases.
[14:45] Priya: Yep — any reduction in variance helps caching. Also consider shorter context windows where possible, that reduces per-request token cost.
[14:56] [16:00] Sofia: Question — can Redwood provide a quick config diff showing current vs recommended?
[16:05] Jordan: Yes, Priya will export a config diff and we will include it in the follow-up.
[16:12] Priya: I'll include the exact batching window changes and which routes to map to 8-bit vs 4-bit.
[16:18] [18:00] Jordan: Quick run-through of next steps — Jordan to share workbook, Priya to run caching warmup and config diff, Liam to send sample prompts. Maya to confirm SOC2 reviewer.
[18:30] Maya: Sounds good. One more ask: can you add a column in the workbook for tokens per $ normalized to business unit? We want a simple KPI for finance.
[18:36] Jordan: We'll add a normalized column and a short blurb in the sheet explaining the normalization.
[18:45] [20:00] Priya: Any other blockers?
[20:03] Ravi: I just need the warmup playbook and the infra limits for KV mem size.
[20:08] Priya: We'll include recommended memory/eviction settings in the warmup deliverable.
[20:14] [22:00] Jordan: Ok if no other blockers we'll wrap. Thanks everyone.
[22:05] Maya: Thanks, appreciated.
[22:08] Liam: Thanks all.
[22:15] Jordan: I'll follow up with notes, links and the workbook — look for email by EOD.

Recap (from meeting notes):
- Current avg tokens/$ ~1,250 baseline; caching moved that to ~1,640 (approx +30%).
- Batching window increases tokens/$ but raises p95 latency; sweet spot for interactive routes is 10-15ms with 8-bit quantization.
- Proposed tests: 6-hour cache warmup for Top-50 queries; 2-hour 5% canary for new routing; quantization split per-route.
- Compliance: SOC2 docs + KMS support available; Maya to confirm reviewer.

Shared artifacts referenced: tokens workbook (drive link), prelim warmup playbook (attachment to follow-up), SOC2 artifact pack (internal link).

End of transcript.
